entities.name: Flaithbertach mac Loingsig
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Flaithbertach mac Loingsig, who died in 765 CE, presided as High King of Ireland from 728 to 734, representing a pivotal, albeit brief, period of ascendancy for the Cenél Conaill branch of the northern Uí Néill dynasty. His reign marked a complex interplay of dynastic ambition, ecclesiastical influence, and military maneuvering within the fragmented political landscape of early medieval Ireland. As the son of Loingsech mac Óengusso, a previous High King, Flaithbertach inherited a legacy of power struggles, striving to consolidate authority in an era where the High Kingship was more an aspiration than a consistently enforced dominion, often contested by rival Uí Néill branches and provincial kings. His temporary hold on this prestigious title underscores the cyclical nature of power shifts among the Gaelic polities, influencing the political geography of the North.

Flaithbertach ascended to the High Kingship following a period of intense rivalry, notably after the death of Cináed mac Írgalaig. His rule was characterized by efforts to assert dominance over competing Uí Néill factions, particularly the Cenél nEógain, and to secure the traditional rights and tributes associated with the kingship of Tara. A significant event during his reign was the hosting of the 'Law of Adomnán' (Cáin Adomnáin) in 727, a legal code protecting non-combatants, especially women and children, in warfare, which Flaithbertach helped enforce or reaffirm. His military engagements included a notable defeat at the Battle of Fochart in 732 against Áed Allán, the rival king of Cenél nEógain, which ultimately weakened his grip on the high kingship.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Flaithbertach's brief reign as High King confirmed the ongoing, albeit contested, power of the Cenél Conaill and his defeat at Fochart directly contributed to the ascendance of the Cenél nEógain, reshaping the dynastic balance in early medieval Ireland. His association with the Cáin Adomnáin also highlights the intersection of secular and ecclesiastical law.
